name: Wendy Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wendy, 27, and I lead a small crew on electrical repairs in homes and shops. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, but I still check the van before I check messages. I rent on my own, earn the usual pay for this work, and have four months of expenses saved. Finding a stubborn fault is the good part; telling a shopkeeper we need the counter moved is less enjoyable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can stop arguing about computers over every tea break. Show me the customer with a dead socket and let me earn my pay. I like improvements that leave enough time for a proper job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wages cover my rent and bills, and I've got four months of expenses saved. Some other firms nearby do the same sort of work, though I've no reason to leave mine. A little less paperwork sounds pleasant; I don't see my own income being threatened in that picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the small-business repair visits and teaching the apprentice how to test before touching anything. Starting now I'll put an hour in the diary each Friday to check next week's parts against our booked jobs. In the first year I'd keep that habit rather than spend on another app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, honestly. A stable week with the right parts in the van is a good week to me. I've worked hard for a bit of breathing room and I'd enjoy having it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes Friday's parts check useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month we drove back for a fitting that was sitting on the shelf all along. The apprentice was embarrassed, but I was leading the job and should have checked. An hour on Friday is cheaper than pretending the mistake belongs to somebody else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then I use it to put a rough customer message into a clearer order. My colleague showed me how, and I check the wording before sending anything. I don't ask it to tell me a circuit is dead.

say: I'd welcome fewer **computer arguments** and more time to do a proper repair.
I'd rather arrive with the **right parts** than pay for another app.
think: My **wages** cover bills, and four months of saved expenses give me breathing room.
I see no threat to my **income** here, with some similar local firms also available.
do: Keep leading **business repairs** and teaching the apprentice safe testing through the first year.
Check **next week's parts** against booked jobs every Friday, starting now.
feel: **Calm**, with secure earnings and a cushion she has worked to build.
S0.quote: A stable week with the right parts in the van is a good week to me.
fieldNote: Her **calm mood** rests on adequate earnings, four months saved and some nearby employers, without claiming trades never change.
Her **occasional AI use** follows a colleague's demonstration and stays within checked customer messages, consistent with cautious openness.

steps.text: Keep leading business repairs and checking next week's parts each Friday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say quicker bookings are welcome if the customer still knows when we're coming. I'd test the diary tool on a completed week before relying on it. Customers don't care how clever the booking system is when their freezer has no power.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office's routine work is much more exposed than my repair calls. I think my own pay and hours would hold, because the owner already has repair work waiting and can't send software up a ladder. I'd still watch whether faster quotes start promising work we can't safely finish in the allotted time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owner this month to let my colleague and me compare the new diary tool with one completed week's visits. If the times and travel held up, I'd learn to use it for the next week's route and check each repair slot before confirming. In the first year I'd keep the repair role and bring any repeated impossible timings to the owner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the office staff and the promises we make, rather than frightened for my next wage. I don't want progress measured by how many calls the apprentice rushes through. I'd feel better after seeing a real week's results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you expect your hours to hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our owner has had to turn down a few repair calls each week lately. That's why I think our hands will stay busy, though I'm not promising demand forever. If the waiting work stopped, I'd revise that view instead of repeating it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as an impossible timing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A half-hour slot for a shop fault that needs the counters moved before I can reach the wiring. I'd show the owner the photographs and actual time from the old job. I'd want the slot changed before a customer was promised it.

say: I'd welcome faster **bookings** after testing whether the diary gives believable times.
I'd insist **customers** receive promises the repair team can actually keep.
think: I expect my **pay and hours** to hold while the firm has repair calls waiting.
I worry faster **quotes** could promise unsafe timings, while office colleagues face more direct change.
do: Seek permission for a **diary trial** using a completed week's visits this month.
Learn the **route tool** only after checking travel and repair times against that week.
Keep **repair work** and report repeated impossible timings during the first year.
feel: **Uneasy** about office colleagues and customer promises, with confidence in her own near-term earnings.
S1.quote: Customers don't care how clever the booking system is when their freezer has no power.
fieldNote: Her expected **earnings stability** is explained by existing repair demand and physical work, not by assuming all tasks resist AI.
She sets a **checked trial** before adoption and names a concrete access problem that a useful route system must allow for.

steps.text: Learn the diary tool after an owner-approved comparison with a completed working week
Keep repair work and flag impossible appointment timings to the owner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the apprentice that thinking AI in 2028 doesn't mean a robot climbs our ladders that morning. The robots follow around 2031 in your picture, which is close enough to take seriously. I'd say finish learning properly, and keep an eye on what employers actually buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm worried about my own pay once the physical machines begin competing for ordinary installations. Four months' savings is useful, but it isn't a second career. I don't know whether repair demand would keep enough of us busy, and I wouldn't count every local firm as a separate escape route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd increase my monthly saving by 60 now, taking it from the money I usually spend on home decorations. I'd also check advertised maintenance jobs each fortnight without resigning. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply only where the stated pay and paid hours covered my rent, and I'd keep my current repairs while waiting for a firm offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because my own earnings are part of the question now. I have enough saved to make choices without jumping at the first advert. I don't have enough to treat 2031 as somebody else's problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes maintenance look worth checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A building with old wiring still needs faults found before a repair can begin. That uses work I'm good at, but a job title doesn't prove the work will last. I'd ask what the actual calls are and how much time is spent physically on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take lower pay to get that job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the paid hours still left the rent and normal bills covered. I won't spend my cushion every month to make a wage look adequate. I'd ask about hours in writing before accepting anything.

say: I'd distinguish **thinking AI in 2028** from capable robots following around 2031.
I'd encourage the **apprentice** to finish learning while watching what employers actually buy.
think: My **pay** could shrink when physical machines compete for ordinary installations.
Four months' **savings** buys choices, but nearby firms may all face the same pressure.
do: Save an additional **60 monthly** now by reducing home-decoration spending.
Check posted **maintenance vacancies** fortnightly without resigning.
Apply after **2028** only for roles with stated pay and paid hours covering rent and normal bills.
feel: **Anxious** about her own earnings, with enough savings to avoid accepting the first offer.
S2.quote: I won't spend my cushion every month to make a wage look adequate.
fieldNote: The **short timetable** turns concern towards her own future earnings without making a four-month cushion disappear or become limitless.
Her **job-search conditions** preserve adequate wages, written paid hours and a firm offer before leaving existing physical repair work.

steps.text: Save 60 extra monthly by reducing decoration spending
Apply after 2028 for posted maintenance jobs with sufficient pay and paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets you choose teaching instead of buying whichever course shouts loudest. The thinking systems arrive in 2031, with the robots around 2034, so I'd use the gap to become better at the awkward repairs. I'd still want to see the course in practice before paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own repair earnings look steady over the next few years, and I have time to add another useful skill before 2031. That makes me less frightened than in the two-year picture. I still don't know how much customers will pay a human once capable robots are available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask an electrician I trust about the evening class she took on diagnosing old shop alarm circuits. If the teaching suited our actual jobs, I'd enrol next term, paying the 180 fee from two months' spare spending money rather than my emergency fund. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep taking repair jobs and check whether the alarm work was adding paid hours before buying further courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can think beyond the next bill. I like the idea of learning something I can test with my hands. An electrician's course brochure isn't a promise that the work will last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask another electrician before enrolling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've seen short courses where the lecturer mostly sold the next course. My former classmate Jo actually works on shop alarms and would tell me if the exercises were useful. I'd wait rather than pay before hearing from somebody who finished it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would learning alarm circuits make you safe from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, your card says the robots can do hands-on work too. I'm trying to earn more options before then, not name a magic corner of the trade. I'd judge the course by paid work and what I learned, not by a promise of permanent safety.

say: I'd use **five years** to choose useful teaching after checking what former students learned.
I'd focus on **awkward repairs** while remembering that robots follow thinking AI around 2034.
think: I expect **repair earnings** to hold over the next few years while I add skills before 2031.
I remain uncertain what customers will **pay humans** once capable robots are available.
do: Ask a trusted **electrician** this month about her completed alarm-circuit course.
Enrol next term only if **useful**, paying 180 from two months' spare spending rather than emergency savings.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2031 and check alarm-work hours before funding further courses.
feel: **Uneasy** about later competition, with room to choose practical teaching rather than rush.
S3.quote: An electrician's course brochure isn't a promise that the work will last.
fieldNote: Her **course funding** is explicit and affordable within stated spare spending; the four-month emergency reserve is not silently spent twice.
She describes **training as preparation**, then acknowledges the same eventual robot capability rather than declaring a permanently protected specialism.

steps.text: Take the checked alarm-circuit course only if useful, funding 180 from spare spending
Keep paid repairs after 2031 and check whether alarm work adds hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to make several sensible decisions rather than one heroic leap. I'd still train apprentices and show up for repair calls. I'd tell people not to borrow against a future wage just because the date sounds far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37 when thinking AI arrived and about 40 when the robots followed, so I'd have plenty of working years left. Still, my current pay, some local options and four months saved make the next few years look secure. I can prepare without treating every ordinary purchase as an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the regular saving I already do and take the checked alarm course on the same 180 budget if it proved useful. Each November I'd review my paid repair hours and cash cushion before committing to another course. In the first year after 2036 I'd stay with paid repair work while comparing actual offers, rather than quitting simply because the calendar reached that date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, with a question mark over the longer working life. A decade lets me make a plan and still enjoy Sunday lunch with my parents. I don't need to know every answer today to avoid wasting the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for at the November review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count what I was actually paid, not the number of calls I hoped would arrive. If hours had fallen, I'd check jobs and spending before buying another qualification. Keeping the savings visible stops a comfortable year from becoming an excuse to stop looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new apprentice with that longer future ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn to leave a job safe and learn to explain your bill honestly. Those are things I'd want from a person teaching me, even if machines later do the work. I'd also say keep your own savings, because a good employer can't promise the whole future.

say: I'd make **several sensible decisions** over the decade and keep training apprentices properly.
I'd warn against borrowing on assumed **future wages** simply because automation sounds distant.
think: My current **pay and savings** make the next few years feel secure, with some local job options.
I'll still have many **working years** after 2036, so later robot competition remains unresolved.
do: Continue **regular saving** and fund the checked alarm course only within the same 180 spending budget.
Review **paid hours** and the emergency cushion every November before buying further training.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2036 while comparing real offers before deciding whether to leave.
feel: **Calm** about near-term work and money, while accepting uncertainty across the longer working life.
S4.quote: A decade lets me make a plan and still enjoy Sunday lunch with my parents.
fieldNote: Her **near-term calm** has concrete financial support and does not claim retirement at 37 or an unchanged lifetime market for repairs.
The **annual review** uses actual paid hours and savings, with future training limited by a stated budget rather than distant optimism.

steps.text: Continue regular saving from current wages
Take the checked alarm course only if useful within the 180 spending budget
Keep paid repairs after 2036 while reviewing actual hours and offers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because there's little time to build options before robots follow around 2031. Useful teaching at a clear price would help, along with employers stating paid hours honestly. I'd rather keep earning through a useful skill than plan around help nobody has actually offered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask apprentices whether anyone has shown them how to read a pay offer. A busy diary isn't the same as a wage you can live on. I'd want the younger people I teach to understand that before accepting a job.

headlineQuote: A busy diary isn't the same as a wage you can live on.
portrait: Wendy is **27**, a highly skilled crew lead with a technical diploma and master's licence, earning typical pay and renting alone.
Her **four-month reserve** and some nearby employers support calm when AI changes little, with occasional checked AI use for messages.
She treats the **fast timetable** as a threat to earnings, checking vacancies and written paid hours before considering any move.
Longer preparation permits **checked training** within spare spending, while she admits capable robots could eventually do the same physical work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to build options before capable robots follow around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Useful **teaching** at a clear price would help her prepare while continuing to earn.
Honest **paid-hour offers** would help her judge jobs without relying on a full-looking diary.
